definition.text: Governance, as a cross-cutting concern, is the platform's continuous compliance-and-audit posture applied across the whole journey, not the single decision this repo already profiles separately at card 2.2 Policy. This repo's own target architecture states cross-cutting guarantees generally as something the platform applies rather than something a caller asks for: "Telemetry, policy, provenance and budget are applied by the platform, not requested by the caller" (F-b1-08), consulted at every entry point per this repo's own owner document (T-t2-03). Policy's own contract, by contrast, is one point-in-time call: "Refusal is deterministic and happens before execution, not after spend" (F-b4-04) -- an admit/deny answer for one action. Two legs of what Governance adds beyond that single call are directly evidenced in this pass: a compliance mapping to a named external framework, since ISO 42001's clauses map closely onto the EU AI Act's Articles 9-17 obligations (X-end-to-end-050), and a tamper-evident audit record naming the actor behind every decision (X-maturity-b-004). A third leg -- that Governance also covers who may read or change the governing rules themselves -- is this repo's own proposed reading, not sourced to any record found in this pass; it is named here as a plausible boundary against Policy, not an evidenced one.

landscape.text: The market signal is that governance is now sold as a layer bundled across everything, not a standalone product: "Industry analysts now identify AI Agent Management Platforms as the emerging solution, a centralized control plane that unifies governance, security, observability, and operational oversight across the full agent estate" (X-end-to-end-073). Its enforcement mechanics are stated as a general cross-cutting-architecture pattern, not a domain-specific rule: "Authorization is a cross-cutting concern where enforcement must be interposed at every action and consult policy-relevant context accumulated across the execution" (X-xc-enforcement-chain-006). A published maturity scale exists for governance posture specifically -- OWASP's Agentic AI Maturity Model runs level 0 ('no formal recognition of agentic risk') through level 4, whose top tier includes "real-time anomaly detection, working kill switches, and governance enforced as machine-readable policy" (X-refmodel-rail-7-operations-008) -- but it grades security/governance posture generally, not an audit-record format. And the wire protocols a governed agent actually runs over cannot carry the decision themselves: "Current protocols can transport governance-related messages as opaque payloads (e.g., via A2A task messages or MCP tool calls), but cannot interpret, validate, or enforce their governance semantics" (X-entry-composition-059) -- governance has to be enforced underneath the protocol, not by it.

usage.text: Because this is a cross-cutting concern there is no single 'governance call': the same platform-applied posture this repo states for every cross-cutting guarantee -- "Telemetry, policy, provenance and budget are applied by the platform, not requested by the caller" (F-b1-08) -- and the same reach across every entry point this repo's own target document states -- guarantees "managed across the entire structure, whichever entry point was used" (T-t2-03) -- apply to Governance too. Concretely that means three things recur at every step regardless of which door a unit entered through: the rule in force is checked against a named compliance mapping (ISO 42001/EU AI Act obligations, per X-end-to-end-050); the decision and the actor who made it are written to a tamper-evident audit record naming identity, action, outcome and scope (per X-maturity-b-004); and who may read or change the governing rules is itself access-controlled -- a posture the whole journey runs inside, not one call before or after it.

gaps.what: Card 2.2 Policy, profiled separately, already flags the reciprocal duplication: its own sub-line ('Guardrails - authN/Z, budgets, safety, compliance') names 'compliance' a second time and notes 'Compliance also reappears at rail.2 Governance ... which names Policy a second time too.' This card's own definition proposes a three-part boundary -- compliance mapping, an audit record, and access-control administration -- but only the first two are sourced, and both are sourced to generic industry practice (X-end-to-end-050, X-maturity-b-004), not to anything specific to this repo's own architecture; the third leg is explicitly this repo's own proposed reading. No evidence gathered here shows an adapter-level separation between the two cards: the one named tool (OPA/Rego) is the same engine both cards would run on, and it is itself only claimed, not measured, for either.
gaps.why_it_matters: A boundary asserted in prose but not reflected in any adapter, harness or skill contract is not a settled seam; code written against 'Governance' risks re-deciding the same rule Policy already decided, or vice versa, with no stated rule for which wins.
gaps.research_query: does any harness or skill draw a working distinction between a Policy decision call and a Governance compliance/audit record, or are they the same call under two names

gaps.what: No adopted standard exists for the audit-record wire format Governance's own sub-line requires. The one IETF individual draft found for it (draft-sharif-agent-audit-trail) is not an adopted RFC and has no directory under standards/ in this repo; this repo's own standards registry marks both iso-42001 and eu-ai-act 'watch' rather than adopted.
gaps.why_it_matters: Compliance mapping (ISO 42001/EU AI Act) tells a caller what must be recorded, but nothing in the evidence gathered here fixes the shape of the record itself, so two implementations of 'audit trail' here would not be comparable.
gaps.research_query: has draft-sharif-agent-audit-trail or any successor reached RFC status, and does any production agent platform implement it verbatim

gaps.what: Unlike card 2.2 Policy, which has a measured harness result ('passed 45, failed 0'), no harness or example in this repo demonstrates a compliance mapping, an audit record, or an access-control administration flow. This card's status of 'planned' is accurate and unqualified by anything built.
gaps.why_it_matters: Without a runnable check, 'Governance' names an intent, not a capability a caller can rely on; this should not be conflated with Policy's own measured (if narrower) result.

gaps.what: The evidence that wire protocols cannot enforce governance semantics themselves (X-entry-composition-059) does not identify which of this repo's own enforcement points -- admission, dispatch, or the xc-guarantees chain -- is meant to own Governance specifically, as distinct from Policy's already-named enforcement point (the tool gateway, per card 2.2's own usage citation).
gaps.why_it_matters: If Governance and Policy are meant to be enforced at the same point by the same mechanism, they may not be two capabilities at all; if they are meant to differ, no evidence gathered here says where.
gaps.research_query: kb_index.py search "xc-guarantees enforcement point governance versus policy slot"
